title: UK–Germany: The Kensington Treaty, youth links, Brexit effects and security debates
label: 13 October 2026 · Joint session with the German Bundestag
summary: UK and German foreign affairs committees met after leaders signed the Kensington Treaty to discuss how parliaments can hold governments to account and push the treaty into real action. They focused on youth exchanges, practical barriers created by Brexit, economic ties and differing German party views on Ukraine, defence spending and diplomacy.

chapters.title: Why the Kensington Treaty matters to parliamentarians
chapters.takeaway: Both committees want to hold governments to account and turn the Kensington Treaty into tangible activity, including parliamentary and civil-society links.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Today we’ve met after the Kensington Treaty was signed. Our aim is to work together as parliamentarians to scrutinise our governments and push the treaty from paper into action.

turns.speaker: Armin Laschet
turns.text: Parliaments have different parties and debates; the treaty was meant to add a parliamentary dimension to government co‑operation so we can talk about Ukraine, the economy and our future relations.

turns.speaker: Fleur Anderson
turns.text: We want close ties with Europe and with Germany. The treaty covers defence, economy, climate, youth exchanges and more—parliaments should help ensure delivery.

turns.speaker: Jürgen Hardt
turns.text: We wanted a friendship treaty after Brexit. Kensington gives government co‑operation plus a parliamentary and civil society pillar. That’s what we asked for.

chapters.title: Youth, school trips and building long-term ties
chapters.takeaway: All sides flagged youth exchanges as vital; practical fixes like a student travel list and a formal UK–Germany parliamentary exchange were proposed.

turns.speaker: Fleur Anderson
turns.text: I'd like school trips to be visa-free again so young people can build those lifelong memories—this matters as much as defence and trade for the future relationship.

turns.speaker: Awet Tesfaiesus
turns.text: Visiting another country while young creates lasting ties. I worry we’ve lost some closeness since Brexit; restoring school exchanges is important.

turns.speaker: Jürgen Hardt
turns.text: Teachers struggled when every pupil needed a passport. I’ve heard of a new ‘list’ system where a class list suffices; I’ll check whether it works in practice.

turns.speaker: Stephan Mayer
turns.text: We should build a small parliamentary exchange like the US Congress programme, and start a British‑German youth work organisation similar to those with France or Poland.

turns.speaker: Fleur Anderson
turns.text: Good—those are practical ideas for turning the treaty into programmes people experience.

chapters.title: Brexit’s practical effects and the question of rejoining
chapters.takeaway: German speakers warned leaving the EU weakens bargaining power and burdens UK businesses with EU rules; British MPs warned reopening the referendum debate risks political division.

turns.speaker: Edward Morello
turns.text: The PM wants closer ties with the EU. Is full membership an option, or are there other ways the UK and EU—especially Germany—should cooperate more closely?

turns.speaker: Armin Laschet
turns.text: It depends on politics. But the world changed after 2016: competition with China and Russia means Europe needs the single market’s power; the UK matters and we must find close ways to work with it.

turns.speaker: Jürgen Hardt
turns.text: Sovereignty can gain leverage by acting together. Germany’s trade interests are handled at EU level; being in a single market gives stronger negotiating power than any single country alone.

turns.speaker: Fleur Anderson
turns.text: There will be different views in our parliament. Repairing Brexit’s obvious problems, like SAFE, is urgent—sometimes the EU says no and that blocks practical fixes.

turns.speaker: Stefan Keuter
turns.text: My party congratulated the UK on leaving the EU. We favour reform of the EU and are interested in whether your country might want closer ties or rejoining; I’ve heard varied views.

turns.speaker: Aphra Brandreth
turns.text: We had a democratic referendum. Reopening that fight could hold us back from practical cooperation; we should focus where we can work together now, like security and energy.

turns.speaker: Alex Ballinger
turns.text: Businesses have struggled exporting to the EU; many products now must meet EU rules, so small firms effectively follow EU standards without a vote on them—people notice the costs.

turns.speaker: Jürgen Hardt
turns.text: Exactly—if the UK follows EU rules without being at the table, people may later decide being in the decision-making process is better. Our door is open, but it's the UK's choice.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Some of us think Brexit was a mistake, and there will be a public debate. But in the meantime we need Brussels to give tangible results so voters see benefits from closer ties.

chapters.title: Security, Ukraine and differing German views
chapters.takeaway: All agreed the UK–Germany partnership is vital for security, but German parties disagree over arms, diplomacy and social trade-offs; committee members urged both military support and a push for negotiations.

turns.speaker: Dan Carden
turns.text: We’ve strengthened working relations for security since Brexit. Can parliamentary dialogue in Europe focus on making post‑Brexit cooperation meet our security challenges more effectively?

turns.speaker: Lea Reisner
turns.text: My party supports Ukraine but stresses we also need to work out how to end the war—more diplomacy and mediation—not just rearmament. Climate and social security matter too.

turns.speaker: Stefan Keuter
turns.text: Our Opposition view is that the conflict began earlier and that buying cheap Russian gas would help reduce energy pain at home; we don’t see this as ‘our war’ in the same way.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do you accept Germany was a guarantor of Minsk? If energy ties were restored with Russia, what happens to Ukraine?

turns.speaker: Stefan Keuter
turns.text: I don’t deny the war is wrong. I’m saying the roots are older, and political context matters; I argue for realistic debate on energy and costs for our people.

turns.speaker: Adis Ahmetović
turns.text: We stand with Ukraine. But German society’s support has fallen and right‑wing or left‑populist parties exploit that. We must show socially that supporting Ukraine doesn’t mean cutting vital domestic programs.

turns.speaker: Jürgen Hardt
turns.text: Our strategy should be to strengthen Ukraine so Putin faces the prospect of failure and comes to negotiations. We also need the UK in NATO procurement and defence cooperation—UK industry matters.

turns.speaker: Alex Ballinger
turns.text: Across UK politics there’s unity in backing Ukraine. It’s vital we keep that, while also tackling costs for households and businesses.

turns.speaker: Lea Reisner
turns.text: Security is broader than weapons; an ICU nurse, or a single parent worried about rent, has a form of security too. We must balance defence spending with social protection.

turns.speaker: Armin Laschet
turns.text: There are real differences in German parties—some oppose weapons. But our government says: support Ukraine as needed. We also need to reassert European diplomacy so we aren’t sidelined on big talks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. This historic joint session showed many areas where we can collaborate—youth links, trade fixes, defence cooperation and shared diplomacy—and where national politics shape different priorities.
